Uthman ibn Affan, may God be pleased with him — and he was the successor of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and the leader of the Muslims, and they were wronging him, and they besieged him and killed him in the sacred month in the sacred land, wronged, may God be pleased with him — he was asked, when they had withheld water from him while he was in the house, and it was said: "Why do they treat you with this treatment?" and he said: "Falsehood has shown me to them as a devil" — meaning: falsehood has made me a devil in their eyes.

For they did not look at his precedence in Islam, nor at his rights, nor at his trials in Islam, nor at the testimony of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, for him by name to the Garden, nor at the fact that God's greatest good pleasure, after which there is no anger, had come down upon him, so that all his sins are forgiven and forgiveness preceded them. They looked at none of this; rather they began to look at him as a human being like themselves — indeed they supposed him worse than themselves — and appraised him only by some deeds which they saw, and left what stood against them of the immense, great deeds which they neglected. This is what error in the appraisal of people arises from.

Then, supposing that you did look at some faults for a purpose recognised in the revealed law, such as the appraisal of the transmitters of hadith, for example, and of the bearers of knowledge — you must also be a man of scrupulousness and a man of restraint of tongue, and must not exceed the measure that the evidence establishes and the proof establishes.

Yahya ibn Main, may God have mercy on him, said: "We speak about people who may have set down their saddles in the Garden a hundred years ago; but that they should be our adversaries is dearer to us than that the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, should be our adversary."

Whoever looks at the conditions of those who speak in the appraisal and criticism of transmitters among the leaders of the religion finds a great deal of precision and eagerness not to exceed or transgress. The one who is described as "trustworthy" — they cannot deny him his right and describe him as "truthful"; and the "truthful one who does not err" — they cannot describe him as one who errs. And whoever is characterised by one of the ranks of criticism likewise cannot be brought down by them to the rank below it. For that reason the ranks of criticism with them are eight, and each of these ranks has a group particular to it; and one who is criticised cannot be described by a rank of criticism lower than his own, because that is a wrong against him and a transgression upon him — so he is not moved beyond his place.

And it has come in the report of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, that the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, commanded them to put people in their proper places. This entails not moving a person beyond whatever stage he is at.

Then, dealing with them also, in respect of their precedence in Islam and their trials in it, entails the forgiving of many of their slips and errors — as Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, said: "The slips of the scholars are filth, and they are seas; and when water reaches two qullahs it does not carry impurity."

If you look at their precedence in Islam and their trials in it, and how much they taught and how much good they did and how much they prayed and how much they gave in charity and how much zakat they paid and how much they remembered God and how many times they completed the Qur'an — and every letter of it carries ten good deeds — you see the great excellence and the abundant precedence by which they went ahead. And you know that whoever learned from them, they have his reward after their death.

For the generations that preceded us — the generation that preceded us, whom we lived to see and who died, may God have mercy on them — they have the reward of our deeds and the deeds of whoever learned from us until the Day of Resurrection. So they are more excellent than us and better than us, because our deeds are in the scale of their good deeds; and the generation that preceded that is more excellent than that, because the deeds of those are in the scale of their good deeds also; and so on. For this reason the predecessors take precedence over those who come after, because of the increase of reward.

Shaykh Muhammad Ali, may God have mercy on him, said:

*And every reward accruing to the martyrs or to others, such as the scholars and the ascetics, the like of it accrues to the Prophet, over and above the rewards of what the Prophet himself did — together with an added number that is not bounded, and which none can reckon but the One. For every rightly guided person and every doer of deeds, until the Day of Recompense, his teacher has obtained for himself reward like the reward of the doer; and the double of this from the deficient and the complete. And his teacher's teacher has twice that, and four times for the third who follows him; and thus the multiplication of every rank, up to the Messenger of God, of lofty rank, God bless him and grant him peace. And from here is known the preferring of the predecessors and their precedence, in their excellence, over those who came after.*

The evidence for this is his words, God bless him and grant him peace: "Whoever calls to guidance has its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without that diminishing anything of their rewards. And whoever calls to misguidance bears its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without that diminishing anything of their burdens."

Likewise, in a person's dealing with people, he must realise their diversity and the diversity of his need of them. Some of them — his dealing with them is a religious dealing: he prays with him and so helps him in this great rite; he learns with him and so benefits him in the rulings of his religion; he enjoins right upon him if he falls short in it; he forbids him wrong if he falls into it; he reminds him if he is heedless; he helps him if he remembers. This kind of person is in the position of food, of which a person is never independent; and his dealing with him must be surrounded with much sanctity, because it is a religious dealing.

This person — your dealing with him is a religious dealing. So if you see him in any shortcoming, there are no barriers between you and him: you remind him of God; and if he sees you in a shortcoming he reminds you of God. Your relationship with him is not tied to lineage nor to worldly interests; rather it is tied to the sacred religion. And from here it is a relationship that is not cut off.

If he wrongs you or deals with you badly, you will seek an excuse for him and will know that this may be due to some of your own evil deeds, whose punishment was hastened to you when there ran upon this person's tongue an address to you of what is unfitting, or a treatment of you in what is unfitting; so at that point you will look at yourself from this angle.

If any ill proceeds from him towards you while you know nothing of him but good, do not be hasty against him; and seek an excuse for him — that he may be angered for some reason, or that your understanding may be mistaken in some respect, or that he may be afflicted with an illness at that time. So you excuse him, just as there befalls you yourself of weakness and of turbidity; for your own states are not fixed, and in every hour there pass over you such changes as indicate passing away and departure from this abode. So likewise you must excuse others for what befalls them of contingencies and states.

The brave man, if he flees once, that is no disgrace upon him, because bravery was known of him before, as the poet said:

*And fleeing today is no disgrace upon the young man, if bravery was known of him yesterday.*

And likewise the swift horse, if it stumbles once, is excused in that. "Overlook the stumbles of people of standing."

God, glorified and exalted, has set out a great deal of this dealing and its aspects. Among them is what relates to asking permission to enter, when He said: {And if it is said to you: Go back — then go back; it is purer for you} (Sūrat al-Nūr 24:28). This is a most remarkable aspect: if you ask permission of your neighbour and your intimate friend and he does not permit you, then go back, for it is purer for you. So you are rewarded, and what you were seeking of good — whether worldly or otherworldly — you have obtained more than it, because God, exalted be He, made clear that what you have obtained is purer than what you were seeking. {So go back; it is purer for you} — that is, your going back is purer for you.

And likewise concerning suppositions, God, exalted be He, said in the affair of the slander: {Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and the believing women not think well of their own selves and say: This is a manifest slander? Why did they not bring four witnesses to it? Then, since they did not bring the witnesses, those in the sight of God are the liars} (Sūrat al-Nūr 24:12–13).

Here He said: "did the believing men and the believing women not think well of their own selves" — and what is meant by "their own selves" is their brothers, that is, the believing men and the believing women. So a person must set what has occurred to his mind, that his brother has fallen into it, against himself. If it is possible for it to occur from him, then let him excuse the other and let him know: the matter could happen from me myself, so how should I not excuse the other for its happening from him? And if he finds it impossible, that it could not occur from him, then he ought to seek an excuse for his brother and think good of him, and that this could not occur from him.

{Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and the believing women not think well of their own selves} — that is, why did the believing men and the believing women not think well of their own selves, meaning of the believing men and the believing women, and say: This is a manifest slander? This is the basic principle: that a person should declare it false, because he has the circumstantial evidence that requires declaring it false.

Then it is upon a person, in balance in his own works also, to realise that many of his works may show contradiction or conflict outwardly; but there must be understanding in dealing with them so that that does not occur. In his seeking of knowledge and his seeking of this world, a person often supposes this to be contradictory and conflicting.

Even the Imam al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, when he came to Medina, bought a donkey to move about on between the lessons and the shaykhs; and feeding it and seeking after it wearied him, so he said: "How can one who has a donkey study?" — and he sold it. Then he went on his feet between the study circles and grew tired, so he said: "How can one who has no donkey study?" — and he went back and bought it.

So likewise in the affairs of this life, this sort of thing must occur; and a person aims straight and comes near and strives for the nearest of them to God, glorified and exalted, and the most pleasing to Him. And if he is always, in all his affairs, seeking God's help, exalted be He, and disavowing his own power and strength, then he is helped inevitably:

*If God's help is a companion to a man, then what he wants is made ready for him out of every difficulty; and if there is no help from God for the young man, the first thing that works against him is his own striving.*

And likewise is the case with regard to weighing calling to God against work. There is no doubt that God has made obligatory upon a person calling to His path, and has made clear that his belonging to the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, is conditional upon that: {Say: This is my way. I call to God upon clear insight, I and whoever follows me. And glory be to God; and I am not of those who associate partners with Him} (Sūrat Yūsuf 12:108). So belonging to the following of the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, is conditional upon calling to what he brought.

But many people are prevented from that by the constriction of their time — for the obligations are more than the hours — and he supposes that this work may be undertaken by another, and so entrusts it to that other. And this is part of the lack of balance. So it is upon a person to be balanced: he does not give the whole of his time to calling, for that is a falling short in some of the obligations; and he does not empty the whole of his time of calling, for that too is a falling short in some of the obligations.

So the one who takes the earlier view of moderation in dealing with people — if he looks at them always with the eye of concealment, so that even if he sees the wrong he does not change it and does not enjoin the right, this one is not moderate. He must be moderate: he does not investigate and search out the wrong, but if he sees it he must change it, and the zeal for his religion must take hold of him, and he must come to God's aid, glorified and exalted. He must, if he sees a wrong, change it — but it is not for him to seek it out and search for it.

So it is upon a person to strive for the setting right of himself and the setting right of others as much as he is able, with balance and moderation.

From here, his balancing of his professional performance and his worldly work against the seeking of knowledge and calling to God and the affairs of the hereafter is of this sort. He must divide his time and make his programme ordered: what of it is for the seeking of knowledge is particular to it and is an ordered portion not encroached upon; and what of it is for the seeking of this world is likewise assigned and is an ordered time not encroached upon; and what is for worship is likewise ordered and not encroached upon; and what is for dealing with people and rendering their rights to them is likewise complete and not encroached upon — so that he renders to each holder of a right his right, as far as he is able to find a way to that.

The like of this is what relates to what newly arises of events and matters in people's lives. Many people study jurisprudence, for example, which was set down in ages past, and those who set it down were affected by their own reality. So if you study, for example, in a book among the books of jurisprudence in any of the schools, some rulings, you will find that they relate to speaking of a standing Islamic state in which the prescribed limits of God, glorified and exalted, are established, and His obligatory duties are observed, and His enemies are fought, and all the rites of the religion are established — this is what you study in jurisprudence. And you find certain rulings built upon that.

For example, if you study in the chapter on bringing dead land to life — "and it does not require permission, unlike the near land" in the Mukhtaṣar of Khalil: "and it does not require permission, unlike the near" — that is, dead land far from the settlement does not require the permission of the holder of authority, unlike land near the settlement, which does require the permission of the holder of authority. Then you suppose that the situation is continuing and unvarying, and that our case today is like the earlier case. And from here you suppose that if you are in the popular quarters which have not yet been apportioned, you cannot take a mosque there.

Indeed, some of those who give legal opinions rely upon this text and give the opinion that the mosques which are in the popular quarters that are called "al-kazrah" — that is, taken by force — are usurped mosques in which one does not pray. This is the utmost in poor understanding, because he took a text that follows upon a past situation and a state that has passed, and wanted to apply it today to a completely different matter.

And likewise the case with regard to those who study the reports on the imamate and what relates to it, and the rulings concerning the imams and obedience to them, and want to apply that to elected presidents, supposing that the relation between the voter and the candidate is like the relation between the one commanded and the commander. This is an analogy of wine to milk, and it is the utmost in error and remoteness.

For the successor of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, to whom the Muslims pledged allegiance by right and who undertook the establishing of the religion and the governing of the religion by it — his rights are those stated in the texts of the revealed law. As for what is other than that, such as the presidents of the territories when the Muslim community is cut up into states, as is our case today — not one of them can claim that he is the successor of the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace; for if he claimed that, there would become obligatory upon him such obligations as he cannot undertake — such as fighting the enemy, and establishing the prescribed limits over the whole earth, and justice among all the Muslims, the far of them and the near, their east and their west and their south and their north. And this he cannot do and does not claim.

So if that is known, it is known that the difference in rulings between the two classes is vast — between the rulings concerning presidents and kings and the rulings concerning imams and caliphs; a vast difference between the two classes in rulings and in obligations and in rights. And there must be balance and moderation in this kind of thing.

So too, dealing with rulers in general: among people there is one who is negligent in it and among them one who is excessive. Among people there is one who holds that every ruler is a caliph whose obedience and sincere counsel are obligatory, even if he beats your back and takes your wealth, and who holds to blind following behind every governor. And among them there is one who holds the contrary of that, and holds that all the leaders and presidents of the age are among the tyrants and transgressors — indeed he may pronounce them all unbelievers and so hold that they are all to be openly opposed. And all of this is error.

The middle course is what moderation requires: that they be looked at as not being rightly guided caliphs, and also not being unbelieving atheists, except whoever among them makes unbelief manifest. So they are of the Muslims like others; and their offices are not the office of the caliphate and their rulings are not like the rulings of the caliphate. And this balance and moderation requires that their rights not be transgressed against, and also that they not be sanctified and taken beyond their limit; so they are placed in their appropriate place and are not taken beyond it.

And so in the rest of the rulings, such as the rulings on dealing with the scholars also. For many people are negligent and many of them are excessive. Those who are negligent, if they hear any slip or any statement that contradicts their own inclination and contradicts what they have, from a scholar among the scholars, or from one whom people so describe, cast him off and band together against him and hold that he is an enemy of God and His Prophet, and make him the equivalent of the brothers of apes and swine.

And in contrast to that we find others who sanctify everyone who is associated with knowledge, even if he is not of the people of knowledge. And it is known that this age we are in is the end of this community, in which claimants become numerous and those who claim knowledge and are not of its people become numerous. The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, made that clear. Al-Bukhari and Muslim reported in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, from the report of Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, may God be pleased with them both, that the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said: "God does not take this knowledge away by snatching it away from people; rather He takes it away by the death of its people, until, when He has left no scholar, people take ignorant men as leaders, and they are asked for legal opinions and give opinions without knowledge, and so go astray and lead astray."

So if a person goes to excess concerning them and holds that everyone of whom it is said that he is a scholar, or of whom it is said that he is a giver of legal opinions or a jurist, then what he says is correctness itself and cannot be opposed in any way whatever — this is the view of the Shia, who hold that their reference-authorities are protected from error and that they are imams from whom legislation issues; so they assign to them a right among the rights of divinity, namely legislation.

And it is known that legislation, by way of permitting and forbidding and otherwise, is among the exclusive properties of divinity. None makes lawful and none makes forbidden but God, the Sovereign, the Judge, alone. Whoever is below Him has no right of making lawful nor of making forbidden. The rulings are all from God, glorified and exalted, alone; He is the Judge, the Just, alone. And the Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, is the conveyer from Him; and the scholars are those who set out what the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, conveyed, entrusted with it only. But it is not for any of them to make a forbidden thing lawful nor to make a lawful thing forbidden; and it is only for him to strive in conveying and setting out to people what the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, brought from God, exalted be He.

And if he departs from what the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, brought, then a foot will slip after its firmness, and he will taste evil for having barred from the path of God, as God, exalted be He, said: {And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God, to lead people astray without knowledge?} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:144) — that is, no one is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God to lead people astray without knowledge.

From here they must be looked at with this balanced, moderate view: that they be looked at as a people entrusted with the revelation, so that whoever of them has a greater share of it has a greater share of correctness and deserves esteem — but does not deserve sanctification. So he is esteemed according to the measure of his knowledge and his God-consciousness and his scrupulousness, but he is not sanctified; it is known that he may err. And from here, of his statements, what agrees with the truth is taken and what contradicts it is rejected — as Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: "There is not one of us but that he rejects and is rejected, except the occupant of this grave," God bless him and grant him peace.

The human being upon whom not a single thing can be rejected in this community is Muhammad, God bless him and grant him peace. Those below him, all of them, some of their statements can be rejected. Abu Bakr — you may differ from him in some of his statements, and the Companions, God's good pleasure be upon them, differed from him in some of his independent reasonings; and Umar likewise, and Uthman likewise, and Ali likewise. And if differing from these is possible, how should differing from those below them not be possible?

Ubaydah al-Salmani, may God have mercy on him — and he is among the imams of the Successors and their scholars — said to Ali, may God be pleased with him, when he asked him about the question of the slave mother of a child, and he mentioned that he used to give a legal opinion on it, together with his brethren — that is, with the Companions — in the caliphate of Umar and Uthman, with such-and-such, and that today he had retracted that: he said: "Your statement in company is dearer to us than your statement in separation." And Ali was pleased with that and laughed.

So Ali here approved Ubaydah in rejecting his statement to his face — and he is the caliph and Ubaydah is his student. When he said to him: "Your opinion in company is dearer to us than your opinion in separation," he laughed and accepted that and was pleased with it.

For this reason it must be known that dealing with them is of this sort, and is with the manners of the revealed law. The one who is able to criticise is the one who knows that his level is above the level of the one criticised, or equal to it — this is the one who is able to contend with him and to meet argument with argument. And the one below him must take what is correct and reject what is in error, but he must know his own place in which he is, which God has placed him in, and must not demand to reach a place he has not reached. For the one who adorns himself before people with what is not in him is like one who wears two garments of falsehood.

From here it is upon a person to know that even if he is granted understanding or knowledge in one question or in several questions, or has memorised some of the texts of the revealed law in some matters, that does not mean that he has become a judge over all people. Rather it means that God, exalted be He, has shown him of guidance and light what he distinguishes some of the truth by — and some of it may be hidden from him; and this is among the necessities of being human. Some of the truth may be hidden from him, and he must be conscious of that — that much of the truth may be hidden from him.

God, exalted be He, said to the Jews: "And you have not been given of knowledge except a little" — even though He had given them the Torah, and had written it for Moses with His right hand on the tablets, and in it are many details of many matters; and even so He said: "And you have not been given of knowledge except a little." So we must be conscious of this in dealing with others.

Likewise in dealing with the people of calling to God generally, there must also be this moderation and balance. Everyone who calls to the road of truth — whether in his calling he works individually or collectively, and whether he is contemporary with you or preceded you, and whether his calling is directed to all the segments of society or to some of them — ought to be a place of esteem, because he has discharged a communally obligatory duty and has lifted from you a sin that was upon your own neck with which you would have come before God, and he has undertaken it on your behalf. If you know that, it is upon you to esteem him by the measure of what he has undertaken on your behalf of the obligations. Al-Hutay'ah said:

*Lessen your blame upon them — may your father have no father! — or else fill the place that they have filled.*

This is of justice and fairness. Then it is upon you to know that he at least complied with God's command and discharged some of what is upon him, even if he was incapable and weak, and even if his level was modest — at the least he turned to the road of guidance and strove to make the truth manifest with what strength he had. Even if he stammers over the Book of God, indeed even if he errs in it or in the reports of the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, yet he exerted effort to set them out and to convey them.

So which of the two is better — this one who keeps silent about the truth and does not speak it and does not convey it, or this one who conveys it even if he stammers over it and errs? Which of the two is better? There is no doubt that the one who conveys it and stammers over it is more excellent than the one who keeps silent about it, because the one who keeps silent about it is concealing it. So then the difference between the two classes is vast, and the level is different between them. Hassan, may God be pleased with him, said:

*Do you satirise him when you are no match for him? Then let the worse of you be the ransom for the better of you.*

Then we must know likewise that those who call to God, glorified and exalted, differ in their temperaments and their independent reasonings, and in the services they render and the fields they excel in — for which of men is faultless? There cannot be found one who is able to cover all the obligations of calling and all its scope and all its fields; no one is able to fill that. So whoever fills one aspect of it and is more effective and more beneficial is more excellent than the one who fills less than that; but all of them share in the excellence and are partners in the reward and the gain, according to the measure of what they have offered to the religion and according to the measure of what they have expended of sincere counsel to God and to His Messenger and to the believers.

From here, seeking out their slips and their errors and striving to spread them is all of it a harm to the religion and a diminishing of its service. Even if one of them falls into an error, it is upon you to counsel him kindly, with the recognised counsel, between you and him; and it is not for you to expose him publicly and to announce that to the assembly. For that does not serve the religion but demolishes it; it is a striving to demolish the religion.

When you expose one who strives to help the religion and calls to it, and you expose his errors, the meaning of it is that you are demolishing one of the aspects of the religion while you are not conscious of it — and this is a great danger and a great error. Therefore it is upon you to seek an excuse for them all; and whoever of them errs, you call him and counsel him between you and him.

And if he sets out to you what is correct and you know that what he said has a valid aspect — that what he said has an aspect, even if that aspect is one in a hundred — then excuse him, because he relied upon an evidence, and this is the level of his understanding and the level of his knowledge; while you rely upon another evidence, and the preponderance of his evidence over yours has not become apparent to you. Therefore there must be mutual excusing if agreement is not reached. And if agreement is reached, so that one of you returns to the other, then well and good, and this is preferable and more fitting.

But if agreement is not reached and each holds to his evidence, then all of them are not acting by their own caprices nor of their own accord; rather they are following the evidence they have. And this evidence is the proof and is the judge over them all; and all must submit to the judgement of God and His Messenger, and the Qur'an and the sunnah must be above all. So any disagreement is referred in it to the Book and the sunnah: "And if you dispute in anything, refer it to God and the Messenger, if you believe in God and the Last Day. That is better and more excellent in outcome."

Then after that comes the understanding of those possessed of derivation among those entrusted with the revelation; for God referred to them in His words: {And when there comes to them a matter of security or of fear, they broadcast it; whereas had they referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those of them who derive it would have known it} (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:83).

So "those in authority" are the scholars who derive the rulings, because He said: "those of them who derive it would have known it." So referring to them is an appeal to the judgement of the Book of God and the sunnah of His Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, when hiddenness occurs and the meaning is obscure. For they are the ones who know how to reconcile what appears to conflict, and they are the ones who know the difference between the earlier and the later and between the abrogating and the abrogated and other things. Therefore recourse is had to their derivations and their opinions; and if they agree upon a matter, it is not for anyone to oppose their opinion, because their agreement is a binding proof. And if they differ, that is a latitude and a mercy; so whoever follows any group of them and is convinced by its evidence is saved, and praise belongs to God.

Then among the matters in which moderation and balance are required is what relates to dealing with the household, and especially dealing with women. For manly virtue requires the meeting of everything they ask for of needs, while the religion may stand in the way of that; so there must be moderation and balance between the two matters.

A person must consider that it is not lawful for him to withhold from them a right that God, exalted be He, has made obligatory, and that it is likewise upon him to deal with them with kindness and excellence and to render all the rights. But it is also upon him not to exceed the right established in the revealed law, for exceeding it is not of excellence. And many of those who exceed the limit, supposing that to be excellence, fall into the squandering which God has forbidden and whose people He made brothers of the devils: {Truly the squanderers are brothers of the devils} (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:27). So balance in this is required and moderation in it is indispensable.

Likewise, upon the women too there is a great portion of balance and moderation in dealing with the household, and in rendering the rights of the parents and the rights of the husband and the children and the rights of calling to God and of the neighbours; and it is indispensable. And it requires understanding in religion and a distinguishing of priorities and an ordering of them, and a beginning with the most severe and strongest of them and then with the one that follows.

And we know that Satan is an enemy to us, and that he has set up the nets and the snares in the road, and has set up his nets in order to make a person fall into them. So he strives first to cast him into associating partners with God (shirk) by all his means. If he is unable to do that, he attempts to cast him into the indecencies and the grave sins. If he is unable to do that, he attempts to make him fall short in some of the obligatory duties. If he is unable to do that, he attempts to occupy him with some of the obligatory duties at the expense of others. If he is unable to do that, he attempts to occupy him with some of the sunnah acts at the expense of some of the obligatory duties. If he is unable to do that, he attempts to occupy him with some of the sunnah acts at the expense of others, or to make him fall into the disliked acts (makrūhāt); then into what is contrary to what is preferable (khilāf al-awlā); then into occupying himself with the recommended acts (mandūbāt) at the expense of the sunnah acts which are more excellent than they; then into occupying himself with what is not time-bound at the expense of what is time-bound, until the time of the time-bound act, which takes precedence over others, passes.

Therefore it is upon a person to be alert to these dangers which Satan casts in his road, and to seek refuge in God from him, and to depend upon God and rely upon Him in his whole affair, as the prophets used to do. For their reliance upon God, glorified and exalted, was the occasion of their overcoming all the impediments and obstacles; and they said, as God related of them: {And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us in our ways? And we shall surely be patient with the harm you do us; and upon God let those who rely place their reliance} (Sūrat Ibrāhīm 14:12).

This is the guidance of the prophets, so it is upon us all to be guided by it. And I am not able to trace all the aspects of moderation and balance in the life of the Muslim; and I think that some lessons have already preceded on it which may take in more than this. Even so, a time such as this does not cover it, so I shall confine myself to this limit and take a few easy questions.

flags.arabic: فقال تعالى: {لا يكلف الله نفسا إلى وسعها}
flags.context: Cited as evidence that God does not charge a person beyond his effort.
options: Render the verse in the sense the argument requires and mark the departure, as done here
Restore the verse silently to its Qur'anic wording
Withhold the citation until the source is corrected
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT IN A QUR'ANIC QUOTATION. Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:286 reads 'illā wusʿahā' ('except [with] its capacity'). The published Arabic has 'ilā wusʿahā', substituting the preposition 'ilā' for the exceptive particle 'illā' — one letter, but it makes the clause ungrammatical and destroys the sense. Style guide 11 forbids restoring the wording of quoted scripture, so body_ar preserves the defect and the English marks it. The Sheikh's argument depends on the correct reading. This is a single-letter slip, most probably a transcription error rather than a misquotation by the Sheikh, but it must not be silently repaired.

flags.arabic: فالحد الوسط هو الذي يقتضيه الاعتدال أن ينظر إليهم على أنهم ليسوا بخلفاء راشدين وأيضا ليسوا بكفار ملحدين إلا من أظهر الكفر منهم، فهم من المسلمين مثل غيرهم، ووظائفهم ليست هي وظيفة الخلافة وليست أحكامها كأحكام الخلافة
flags.context: The section on dealing with rulers, following the rejection of analogising elected presidents to caliphs.
options: Translate the middle position exactly, with both exclusions and the exception intact, as done here
Render only the rejection of takfīr of rulers
Render only the denial that they are rightly guided caliphs
flags.note: THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL POLITICAL-THEOLOGICAL PASSAGE IN THIS SLICE, and the one most likely to be excerpted in a distorting way. The Sheikh sets a middle position with FOUR components that must all survive together: contemporary rulers are (i) not rightly guided caliphs, (ii) not unbelieving atheists, (iii) except whoever among them makes unbelief manifest, and (iv) they are Muslims like others whose offices are not the caliphate and whose rulings are not the rulings of the caliphate. He explicitly names and rejects BOTH extremes — blind obedience to every ruler 'even if he beats your back and takes your wealth', and pronouncing them all unbelievers and openly opposing them. An excerpt carrying component (iii) without (ii), or (i) without (iv), would turn a deliberately balancing statement into its opposite. Note also that he grounds this on a refusal to transfer the fiqh of the imamate to elected office — 'an analogy of wine to milk' — which is a usūlī argument about the scope of a ruling, not a political endorsement of either side. The English keeps the reasoning chain intact per style guide 1, and the record should not be excerpted at this point.

flags.arabic: فلا تقع ذنوبهم إلا مغفورة لأن الرضا سبق الذنب، فما يقع منهم فيما بعد بعد وفاة النبي (ص) حتى لو كان من الحروب وقتل النفس التي حرم الله بغير حق سبق ذلك رضوان الله الأكبر
flags.context: On the Companions who were present at Badr and who pledged allegiance beneath the tree.
options: Translate the claim exactly as given, as done here
Qualify the claim in the body
flags.note: A substantial and contested theological claim, stated by the Sheikh without qualification: that God's prior good pleasure with the Companions of Badr and of the Pledge is decisive over whatever they did afterwards, expressly including the civil wars and the killing of protected life without right. This is his position on the fitnah among the Companions, and it is the basis for his instruction not to take sides among them. It is a live point of disagreement between Sunni and Shiʿi theology and carries a clear sectarian charge, which is sharpened by his naming of the Shia later in the same lecture. Style guide 6 forbids adding a caveat he did not give, so the claim stands as he makes it.

flags.arabic: هذا هو نظر الشيعة الذين يرون أن مراجعهم معصومون وأنهم أئمة ما يصدر عنهم تشريع فيجعلون لهم حقا من حقوق الإلهية وهو التشريع
flags.context: On those who sanctify everyone associated with knowledge.
options: Translate the characterisation exactly as given, as done here
Render it in less doctrinally specific terms
flags.note: The Sheikh characterises Shiʿi doctrine as holding the marājiʿ to be protected from error and as assigning them a property of divinity, namely legislation. Shiʿi scholars distinguish sharply between the ʿiṣmah of the imams and the fallible ijtihād of a living marjaʿ, so the characterisation would not be accepted by those it describes. Style guide 1 requires that a position attributed to another school stay visibly attributed, which the English does; style guide 6 forbids correcting him. The sectarian charge should be weighed before publication.

flags.arabic: بل إن بعض المفتين يعتمد على هذا المتن فيفتي بأن المساجد التي هي في الأحياء الشعبية التي تسمى بالكزره أي المأخوذة قسرا هي مساجد مغصوبة لا يصلى فيها، هذا غاية في سوء الفهم
flags.context: The worked example of applying an old fiqh text to a new reality.
options: Translate exactly as given, keeping the local term, as done here
Render 'al-kazrah' descriptively without the local term
flags.note: A specific and pointed refutation of a named legal opinion in circulation in the Sheikh's own country: that mosques built in informally settled quarters are usurped and may not be prayed in. 'Al-kazrah' is a Mauritanian term for such quarters, glossed by the Sheikh himself as 'taken by force'; the English keeps it with his gloss. He calls the opinion 'the utmost in poor understanding'. He names no muftī. The passage is the clearest instance in this slice of his usūlī method applied against a contemporary fatwā — the argument is that a ruling premised on a functioning Islamic polity cannot be transferred unchanged to a different reality — and it is load-bearing for the record. A reviewer should confirm the term and the local reference.

flags.arabic: فمنها الفرائض ومنها السنن ومنها المندوبات، والفرائض منها عينية وكفائية، والعينيات منها مضيق في الوقت وموسع … فإن عجز عن ذلك حاول شغله ببعض السنن عن بعض أو بالوقوع في المكروهات، ثم بخلاف الأولى ثم بالاشتغال بالمندوبات عن السنن التي هي أفضل منها
flags.context: Two places: the hierarchy of obligations, and the closing restatement of Satan's ladder.
options: Map every grade to its fixed English rendering and keep the ordering intact, as done here
Simplify the hierarchy
flags.note: Two ruling-dense passages. In both, the Sheikh treats mandūb, sunnah and farḍ as DISTINCT and ordered grades, and in the closing passage he states explicitly that the sunnah acts are 'more excellent than' the recommended acts — which settles the ordering he intends. Style guide 3 requires that the graded Maliki usage survive, but the glossary renders both mandūb and mustaḥabb as 'recommended', so the English risks flattening a distinction the argument rests on; the same difficulty is flagged at ID 478, where the ladder appears in a fuller form. The ordering of the obligatory duties — individually obligatory with a constricted time, then with an ample time, then communally obligatory — has been rendered with the glossary's fixed terms for farḍ ʿayn and farḍ kifāyah and with the muḍayyaq/muwassaʿ distinction spelled out, since there is no settled English for it.

flags.arabic: وإنما خص الله تعالى الذكران في الميراث بالتضعيف بناء على أمور أخرى ومنها ما كلفهم من التكاليف، فالتشريف على قدر التكليف … لكنه مع ذلك في الوصية وفي الوقف وغير ذلك ساوى بينهم، والإخوة لأم سواء أيضا ذكرهم وأنثاهم في الميراث
flags.context: On justice between sons and daughters.
options: Translate the whole passage, with its obligation of equal treatment and its list of counterparts, as done here
Render only the doubling of the male share
flags.note: A passage certain to be excerpted and therefore at risk of distortion in both directions. Its structure must be kept whole: (i) the doubling of the male share in inheritance does NOT license wronging daughters; (ii) it is OBLIGATORY upon parents to observe daughters' rights exactly as sons' in maintenance, housing, upbringing, supplication, counsel and teaching, 'with no difference'; (iii) the doubling is grounded in countervailing financial liabilities laid on men — blood-money, the bridal gift, maintenance — with the Sheikh stating that a woman owes no maintenance to husband, brother or child even if she is rich and they are poor; and (iv) in bequest and endowment the shares are equal, and uterine siblings inherit equally regardless of sex. The Sheikh gives this as the justice of God and offers no further justification, and none has been added. The rendering of mahr follows the glossary as 'bridal gift', never 'dowry'.

flags.arabic: فالمروءة تقتضي تلبية كل ما يطلبن من الحاجات، والدين قد يحول دون ذلك … لكن عليه أيضا أن لا يتعدى الحق الشرعي فتجاوزه ليس من الإحسان
flags.context: On dealing with the household and with women.
options: Translate exactly as given, as done here
Render the passage in more general terms
flags.note: A short passage whose balance must be preserved: it is NOT lawful to withhold from women a right God has made obligatory; they are to be dealt with kindly and all rights rendered; and at the same time exceeding the right established in the law is not excellence but squandering. The Sheikh does not specify which requests he has in view, and nothing has been supplied. He then places a parallel obligation of balance upon women. Read in English out of context the passage is open to being taken as licence to refuse, which the first clause expressly excludes.

flags.arabic: وقد قال الشيخ محمد عالي رحمه الله: «وكل أجر حاصل للشهدا** …» / «وليس فرار اليوم عارا على الفتى * …» / «إذا كان عون الله للمرء صاحبا** …» / «أقلوا عليهم لا أبا لأبيكمُ** …» / «أتهجوه ولست له بكفء** …»
flags.context: Five passages of verse distributed through the lecture.
options: Render as prose in italics and keep the Arabic in the bilingual pane, as done here
Reproduce the source's asterisk hemistich separators
flags.note: Five quotations of verse. Style guide 4: rendered as prose in italics, with no rhymed English attempted. Three poets are named: Shaykh Muhammad Ali, whose long didactic passage on the multiplication of reward up the chain of teachers is the most substantial and is probably a Mauritanian versification, al-Hutay'ah, and Hassan ibn Thabit. The Muhammad Ali passage runs its hemistich markers inconsistently in the source and contains one run-on where a comma replaces the separator; it has been rendered as continuous sense. The line attributed to Hassan is a well-known one and the Sheikh gives it without a source.

flags.arabic: وقد قال الله تعالى لليهود: وما أوتيتم من العلم إلا قليلا
flags.context: On the limits of any person's knowledge.
options: Report the addressee exactly as the Sheikh gives it, as done here
Note that the verse's addressee is disputed
flags.note: The Sheikh states that Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:85 was addressed to the Jews, which follows the occasion-of-revelation reports about the question on the spirit; the verse's general address is read more broadly by many exegetes. He also cites it here without the curly braces he uses elsewhere for Qur'anic quotation, so the citation is unmarked in the source. Neither point has been corrected in the body.

flags.arabic: وأظن أنه قد سبق فيها بعض الدروس التي قد تستوعب أكثر من هذا … فأقتصر على هذا الحد وآخذ بعض الأسئلة اليسيرة
flags.context: The closing sentence of the record.
options: End the English exactly where the Arabic ends, as done here
Treat the record as an excerpt under style guide 9
flags.note: The lecture ends with the Sheikh saying he will confine himself to this limit and take a few questions. The transcript therefore stops at the end of the lecture proper and does NOT include the question-and-answer session that followed. This is not an excerpt in the sense of style guide 9 — the lecture is complete and does not break off mid-clause, and there is no download link — but a display should not imply that nothing followed. He also refers back to earlier lessons on the same subject which are not in this record.

CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY, on three counts. First, the passage on dealing with rulers states a deliberately balanced middle position with four components and two expressly rejected extremes; excerpting any part of it alone inverts it. Second, the hierarchy of obligations and the closing restatement of Satan's ladder are ruling-dense and depend on the Maliki grading of mandūb below sunnah below farḍ. Third, the record carries a one-letter defect in a Qur'anic quotation (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:286) which is preserved in body_ar and marked in the English.

EDITORIAL REVIEW REQUIRED. Besides the passage on rulers, the record contains the Sheikh's position on the Companions' civil wars, a characterisation of Shiʿi doctrine, a pointed refutation of a named legal opinion circulating in his own country about mosques in informal quarters, a passage on the inheritance shares of sons and daughters, and a passage on dealing with women. All are translated faithfully and none is softened. Style guide 12: publication decisions belong to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

This is the most usūlī record in the slice and its opening third is a sustained argument in legal theory rather than a series of rulings: that the truth is protected and its core undisputed, but that the Lawgiver deliberately left part of the evidence non-definitive in transmission or in indication, so that seeking the truth is itself an act of worship and error within it is excused and rewarded. Everything that follows — the refusal to monopolise the truth, the insistence that a scholar is esteemed and not sanctified, the eight ranks of narrator-criticism, the excusing of the Companions and of later scholars, the refusal to transfer caliphal rulings to modern states — is built on that opening. Style guide 1 requires the reasoning chain be preserved rather than compressed into its conclusions, and it has been.

The lecture's structure is a taxonomy of balance, and it should be displayed so the structure is visible: balance in dealing with God (worship against the rights of self and others; the ordering of obligations), with oneself (spirit against body; the four bodily needs), with the family (parents, children, the household), with neighbours, with people in general (appraisal, concealment, the Companions, the scholars, the callers to God), with rulers, and with newly arisen realities.
